title: A written person's story must fit the table they share: the claims are checked by code and the writer of a new set is briefed with the real tables
request: The owner asked to fix the rule for writing the fresh sealed set, after the route test found practice people whose story the shared table could not hold.
spec: A person who shares a table can state what the story relies on in it; code checks the claims against the real table and refuses a false one; a new set can require the claims; the writer gets a brief generated from the real tables; the sets that exist are untouched.
plan: Measure how widespread the flaw is, from the practice sets and the saved conversations
Make the claims machine-checkable and opt-in, required for the next sealed set
Generate the brief for the writer from the tables themselves

decisions.decision: The claims are opt-in and required only for the next sealed set
decisions.why: the practice sets are pinned by hash and were run on; changing how they are checked would change what they mean

decisions.decision: Claims name values and properties, not only columns
decisions.why: the columns of the existing sets match their tables almost always; the stories broke on city names, destinations and duplicates, which a column check cannot see

decisions.decision: The brief is generated, with a test that it is current
decisions.why: a hand-written brief drifts from the tables, which is how the practice set came to be written for tables nobody had shown the writer

decisions.decision: The practice set is not edited
decisions.why: it is hash-pinned; its flawed people are read as flawed in the record instead

change: dclab_rnd/agent_eval/conversation_exam/table_fit.py, brief.py, WRITING_PEOPLE.md (generated), __init__.py (check_person takes require_claims, REQUIRE_CLAIMS, main passes it); tests/test_conversation_exam_table_fit.py

findings.defect: Practice people written without the tables told stories the tables could not hold, and nothing checked it
findings.scenario: in the route test, r-06 (a company in Turkey sharing the UAE sales table), r-17 (Indian city names cleaned in a table of UAE cities with unique ids) and r-20 (a Peruvian tour operator in a table of Paris and Dubai) each drifted into 'I sent the wrong file'; at least three of eight played people with a table, against about one of twenty-six in the set written with the tables in view
findings.cause: the independent writer never saw the three invented tables, and check_person looked at the record's shape, not at whether the story fits its data
findings.fix: table_claims checked against the real table, required for the next sealed set, and a brief generated from the tables

findings.defect: The first version of the repeated-id claim said a column that repeats all the time never does
findings.scenario: a story claiming that the plan column repeats was answered 'it never does'
findings.cause: the claim was meant for id columns and took any column
findings.fix: the claim is refused for a column not ending in _id, with that reason

findings.defect: A badly shaped claim crashed the check instead of being refused
findings.scenario: a writer's typo such as columns given as a number, values given as a list, or a null made the person checker and the exam's main die with a traceback; a bare string was read letter by letter
findings.cause: the claims were iterated without checking their shape
findings.fix: the shape is checked first and refused as malformed table_claims with the shape it should have

findings.defect: The rule that a new set must carry claims was met by writing empty claims
findings.scenario: table_claims set to an empty object, or to empty lists, passed the required-claims rule, which is the failure the package exists to prevent; a story saying one row per customer on the sales table passed because nothing could be claimed about uniqueness
findings.cause: presence of the key was checked, not that it says anything, and only repetition could be claimed
findings.fix: a required set refuses claims that say nothing, and a unique claim for id columns is checked like the repeated one

findings.defect: Number and yes-no columns could not be claimed, and the check leaned on a pandas detail
findings.scenario: a claim about the cancelled column was refused as having too many values; the text-only test of a column would fail on a newer pandas where text is a string type
findings.cause: only columns of the object type were listed
findings.fix: every column with few distinct values is listed whatever its type, and the number ranges, date spans and a text example are listed for the rest

findings.defect: The brief understated what an advice conversation costs, left out the money, date and number facts of the tables, and did not say how to register a new set
findings.scenario: a run capped from the brief's per-conversation cost would stop in the middle of the advice people; a writer could set a story in another currency or year; the exam's own estimate read EUR 4.3 for a run that cost EUR 1.7
findings.cause: the brief listed values and flags only, and the exam's estimate still priced the judge at its old rate
findings.fix: the brief lists ranges, date spans and a price example, gives the advice cost apart, names the route-trap rule and the registration steps; the estimate uses the measured costs

measurements.name: the stories of the route test's people replayed as claims against the real tables
measurements.gate: the claims of r-17 and r-20 as the stories made them are refused with the reason, a story that fits passes, and the existing sets pass unchanged
measurements.result: r-17's Bombay and Bengaluru and its repeated customers, and r-20's Machu Picchu and Cusco, were each refused naming the values the table holds; a fitting story passed in any letter case; the dev and route sets, 40 and 20 people, are unchanged
limits: the claims of r-17 and r-20 were written afterwards from their stories, as the writer would have written them
a story's claim about the table is only checked when the writer makes it

outcome: The next set cannot be written, or run, with a person whose story the table cannot hold, and its writer is shown the tables. The practice set stays as it is.
lessons: Check what a story claims about its data, not only the shape of the record that holds it
Show the writer the real data; a brief generated from it cannot drift
risks: A writer can claim nothing and write a story that does not fit: the claims are required for the next sealed set, but a story detail left unclaimed is still unchecked
